title: How do you scan Docker images for vulnerabilities before deployment (Trivy, Grype, registry scanning), and how do you manage secrets inside containers securely (not in `ENV`/image layers — mounted secrets/secret managers)?
shortTitle: Scanning Docker Images for Vulnerabilities and Managing Secrets Inside Containers Securely

s1_definition.profdef: Scanning a Docker image means analysing its layers, operating-system packages, and application dependencies against known-vulnerability (CVE) databases before it is deployed, using tools such as Trivy or Grype in the pipeline and continuous scanning in the registry, and failing the build or blocking promotion when severe vulnerabilities are found. Managing secrets inside containers securely means never placing secrets in `ENV` instructions, image layers, or the Dockerfile, because image layers are readable and persistent; instead secrets are provided at runtime as mounted files or environment variables injected by the orchestrator from a dedicated secret manager, kept out of the image entirely, and ideally short-lived and rotated.
s1_definition.analogy: Scanning an image is like the National Bank of India inspecting every component of a new cash-counting machine against a recall list before installing it in a branch; if any part is on the recall list for a known defect, the machine does not get installed. Managing secrets in a container is like the vault combination: you would never stamp it onto the machine's casing (an image layer) where anyone servicing it can read it; instead the branch manager receives it fresh each morning in a sealed envelope that is used and then destroyed (a runtime-mounted secret from the key office). Both practices stop known-bad parts and exposed keys from ever reaching a live branch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Scan images for known CVEs with Trivy or Grype and block severe findings before deploy, and never bake secrets into image layers or ENV; inject them at runtime from a secret manager as mounted files or short-lived variables.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Scanning a Docker image means analysing its layers, operating-system packages, and application dependencies against known-vulnerability (CVE) databases before it is deployed, using tools such as Trivy or Grype in the pipeline and continuous scanning in the registry, and failing the build or blocking promotion when severe vulnerabilities are found. Managing secrets inside containers securely means never placing secrets in `ENV` instructions, image layers, or the Dockerfile, because image layers are readable and persistent; instead secrets are provided at runtime as mounted files or environment variables injected by the orchestrator from a dedicated secret manager, kept out of the image entirely, and ideally short-lived and rotated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Scanning an image is like the National Bank of India inspecting every component of a new cash-counting machine against a recall list before installing it in a branch; if any part is on the recall list for a known defect, the machine does not get installed. Managing secrets in a container is like the vault combination: you would never stamp it onto the machine's casing (an image layer) where anyone servicing it can read it; instead the branch manager receives it fresh each morning in a sealed envelope that is used and then destroyed (a runtime-mounted secret from the key office). Both practices stop known-bad parts and exposed keys from ever reaching a live branch.

**One line to remember:** Scan images for known CVEs with Trivy or Grype and block severe findings before deploy, and never bake secrets into image layers or ENV; inject them at runtime from a secret manager as mounted files or short-lived variables.

sections.s2_technical:
Image scanning works by building an inventory and comparing it to CVE feeds. A scanner like Trivy or Grype inspects the image: it identifies the base OS and its installed packages, and it parses application dependency manifests such as the Maven lockfile inside the image. It then checks every component against vulnerability databases and reports findings by severity (low, medium, high, critical), often with the fixed version if one exists.

Scanning happens at several points. In the pipeline, right after the image is built, you run a scan step such as `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL <image>`, where the non-zero exit fails the build on severe findings so the image cannot be promoted. In the registry, continuous scanning re-scans stored images as new CVEs are published, so an image that was clean last week but is now affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability gets flagged even though it already passed the pipeline. Admission control in Kubernetes can also block images that have not passed scanning or are not signed.

Managing the findings is part of the job. Not every finding is fixable immediately, so you triage by severity and exploitability, fix by upgrading the affected package or base image, and for accepted risks you record an explicit, justified suppression with an expiry rather than silently ignoring it. You also keep base images current, because much of an image's vulnerability surface comes from the base OS.

Secrets must never be in the image. The anti-patterns are `ENV DB_PASSWORD=...`, copying a secrets file into the image during build, or passing a secret as a build argument, because every image layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image and the value persists in the registry forever, even if a later instruction deletes the file. A scanner and a careful review should reject any secret baked into a layer.

Secrets are provided at runtime from a dedicated source. In Kubernetes the app reads a secret from a mounted file or an environment variable injected from a Kubernetes Secret, and better still that Secret is synced from an external manager such as Vault or a cloud secret manager using the External Secrets Operator or a Vault Agent sidecar, so the real value lives in the manager and the cluster pulls it in. Mounted files are often preferred over environment variables because environment variables can leak into logs, crash dumps, and child processes more easily. The strongest pattern is short-lived, dynamically issued credentials, for example Vault generating a database credential that auto-expires, so even a leaked value is useless shortly after.

A senior nuance is defence in depth: scanning, signing (so only images from your trusted pipeline run), and generating an SBOM together give provenance and let you answer exactly what is in a production image and whether it is affected by a new CVE. Another nuance is the build-arg trap: a secret passed as a build argument can still end up in image history, so secret material at build time should use BuildKit secret mounts that are not persisted. A third nuance in banking is least privilege and rotation: each service gets narrowly scoped secrets per environment, they are rotated on a schedule and immediately if exposed, and every access is audited, so a leaked QA credential cannot touch Prod.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India shipped the transfer-service image with a vulnerable version of a serialization library pulled in transitively, and it ran in production until an audit found it. This is exactly the problem pipeline image scanning solves. Trivy fails the build on high or critical CVEs, so the vulnerable image never deploys.

Problem 2 — An image that passed scanning months ago became vulnerable when a new CVE was disclosed for a package it contained, but nobody re-checked it. This is exactly the problem continuous registry scanning solves. Stored images are re-scanned as new CVEs appear, flagging the now-vulnerable image.

Problem 3 — A developer put the production database password in an ENV line in the Dockerfile, so it was readable in every pulled image layer and persisted in the registry. This is exactly the problem runtime secret injection solves. The image holds no secret, and the password is mounted at container start from the secret manager.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation. We will model an `ImageScanner` (Trivy/Grype) that inventories an image's packages, checks them against a CVE database, and fails on high or critical findings; a `SecretInjector` that refuses to bake secrets into the image and instead mounts them at runtime from a `SecretManager`; and a `RegistryScanner` that re-scans a stored image when a new CVE is published. We will scan a vulnerable image (blocked), scan a clean image (passes), reject a baked-in secret, mount a runtime secret, and show a continuous re-scan flagging a newly disclosed CVE. This mirrors real scanning and secret handling.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.scan.ScanSecretsDemo

# Real usage: scan before deploy; mount secrets at runtime (never in the image)
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL registry.bank.local/transfer-service:1.2.0
kubectl create secret generic transfer-db --from-literal=db-password=... # or External Secrets
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a CVE database initially knowing one critical vulnerability, a vulnerable image, a clean image, a secret manager, and a later new CVE disclosure.

Step 1: The scanner inventories the vulnerable image's three packages and checks each against the CVE database. It finds the critical vulnerability in the jackson serialization library, counts one severe finding, and fails the scan, blocking the image from deploying.

Step 2: The scanner inventories the clean image, which uses a fixed jackson version. No package matches a high or critical CVE, so the scan passes and the image is allowed to proceed.

Step 3: A developer attempts to bake the database password into the image with an ENV line. The secret injector detects the secret-bearing ENV and throws a SecurityException, refusing to let the secret into an image layer.

Step 4: The injector instead mounts the secret at runtime. It fetches the value from the secret manager at container start, which the manager logs as an audited issuance, and mounts it as a masked file under /var/run/secrets, so the running container has the secret but the image never did.

Step 5: Later, a new CVE is disclosed for the openssl package that the previously clean image contains. The registry scanner re-scans the stored clean image, now finds the high-severity finding, and raises an alert to rebuild, demonstrating that continuous scanning catches images that become vulnerable after they first passed.

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Build image
    │
    ▼
  ImageScanner (Trivy/Grype)
    inventory packages → check CVE DB
    ├─ HIGH/CRITICAL found → FAIL build (block deploy)
    └─ clean → PASS → push to registry
                         │
                         ▼
             RegistryScanner (continuous)
             new CVE feed → re-scan stored image
             ├─ now vulnerable → ALERT + rebuild
             └─ still clean → ok

  SECRETS (separate, never in image):
    Dockerfile ENV secret → SecretInjector REJECTS (SecurityException)
    SecretManager (Vault) ──runtime──▶ mounted file /var/run/secrets (tmpfs)
       real value stays in manager; container reads it at start; audited
```

```
  │ + rejectBakedSecret(line)│───────▶│ + store / fetchAtRuntime │
  │ + mountAtRuntime(name)   │        └──────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Image + Secret Lifecycle ──────────────

  IMAGE:  [BUILT] → scan? ─fail─→ [BLOCKED] ; ─pass─→ [IN_REGISTRY]
                → new CVE → re-scan → [FLAGGED_REBUILD]
  SECRET: [IN_MANAGER] → mount at start → [IN_TMPFS] → container stops → [GONE]
          (ENV/layer attempt → REJECTED)

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. scanner.passes(badImage)  → CRITICAL → false (blocked)
  2. scanner.passes(cleanImage)→ true (push)
  3. injector.rejectBakedSecret("ENV DB_PASSWORD=...") → SecurityException
  4. injector.mountAtRuntime("db-password") → manager.fetchAtRuntime()
  5. registryScanner.rescan(cleanImage) after new CVE → now fails → alert
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Scanning a Docker image means analysing its layers, OS packages, and application dependencies against known-vulnerability databases before it deploys. I use Trivy or Grype as a pipeline step right after the image is built, with the scanner set to exit non-zero on high or critical findings so the build fails and the image cannot be promoted. I also rely on continuous scanning in the registry, which re-scans stored images as new CVEs are published, so an image that was clean when it passed the pipeline but is now affected by a newly disclosed vulnerability still gets flagged. In Kubernetes I back this with admission control that blocks images which have not been scanned or signed. Findings are triaged by severity and exploitability, fixed by upgrading the package or base image, and for any accepted risk I record an explicit, justified, expiring suppression rather than ignoring it.

Managing secrets inside containers starts with a hard rule: secrets never go into the image. No ENV with a password, no secrets file copied in during build, no secret passed as a plain build argument, because every image layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image and the value persists in the registry forever, even if a later instruction deletes the file. The image contains only code.

Secrets are provided at runtime from a dedicated manager. In Kubernetes the app reads the secret from a mounted file or an injected environment variable that comes from a Kubernetes Secret, and that Secret is ideally synced from Vault or a cloud secret manager with the External Secrets Operator, so the real value lives in the manager and the cluster pulls it in. I prefer mounted files over environment variables because environment variables leak more easily into logs and child processes, and the strongest pattern is short-lived dynamically issued credentials that auto-expire, so even a leaked value is quickly useless.

On the banking project this prevented two real incidents from recurring: a vulnerable serialization library that had shipped to production until an audit found it, which Trivy now blocks at build time, and a database password someone had put in a Dockerfile ENV, which we removed entirely so the image holds only code and the password is mounted at container start from Vault. The senior points I always add are defence in depth with scanning plus image signing plus an SBOM so I can prove exactly what is in a production image and whether it is affected by a new CVE, using BuildKit secret mounts rather than build arguments so no secret lands in image history, and least privilege with per-environment scoping, rotation, and full audit logging so a leaked QA credential can never reach Prod.
